newsitem.title: UK: POLL-OPINION SPLIT ON COURSE OF UK INTEREST RATES.
newsitem.headline: POLL-OPINION SPLIT ON COURSE OF UK INTEREST RATES.

text.p: Expert opinion is split between those who believe British official interest rates have peaked and those who think the Bank of England may have to raise rates again to squeeze inflation, a Reuters poll showed.

A survey of 26 London-based economists, conducted after the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised official rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent, showed that the largest group, of nine, thought the current cycle had found its upper limit.
"We certainly don't think another move is necessary. The economy is already peaking out and inflation will head lower," said Mark Hale of Sakura.

"The signal in the market right now is quite clear and it has been almost a pre-emptive strike from the Bank of England to sedate inflationary pressures," said Rosanne Maddalena, senior economist at San Paolo Bank.
In a statement accompanying Thursday's rate decision, the MPC delivered a strong hint which bears out the expectations of this group of economists.

The committee, empowered by the Labour government to set rates independently, implied it would not be tightening policy again for some time, saying that "interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target."

Until now, Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who chairs the MPC, has expressed concern that rampant consumer spending fuelled by a recent spate of building society flotations would fan the flames of inflation.
Sterling, recently at eight-year highs against the mark, crumbled after the MPC announcement, as the market took the statement to mean that the rate cycle had peaked.
The pound traded at 3.0120 marks before Thursday's statement but tumbled immediately to 2.9640. The retreat continued on Friday with sterling/mark at 2.9525 around mid-morning.

All remaining contributors to the poll, however, thought that the central bank would be forced to raise rates again. Six said they expected a 25 basis point increase to 7.25 percent, five of them predicting the rise would happen in the fourth quarter.
"Seven (percent) should have been the peak, but because of the risks involved which are on the upside, I am adding another quarter," said Trevor Williams, senior economist at Lloyds TSB Group.
Four contributors said they expected rates to peak at 7.5 percent during the first three months of 1998 and one predicted 7.75 percent would be the upper limit in the third quarter of next year.
Five economists said the MPC was still underestimating inflationary pressures and would therefore be forced to raise rates to eight percent around the middle of next year.

"We doubt seven percent will be enough to subdue the consumer...There is bound to be a rebalancing of the currency and interest rates will have to be rebalanced," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust.
One expert, Richard Jeffrey of Charterhouse, said he saw the peak at 8.5 percent early next year.

"They will have to go significantly higher than current levels. If the intent was to hold sterling then it was a foolish thing to have done. It is never wise for central bankers to get into a debate with the currency markets," he said.
